paragraphs: We now enter the coal and iron country; everywhere are marks of manufacturing life; the cinder heaps form mountains; the earth is seamed with excavations; tall furnaces belch forth flames. We are nearing Manchester. In the bronzed sky at sunset a strangely-shaped cloud hangs over the plain; under this motionless covering are hundreds of bristling chimneys, as tall as obelisks; a huge and black mass is next distinguishable, then endless rows of buildings, and we enter the Babel of bricks.

Walked through the city; seen close at hand, it is still more dismal. The air and the soil appear charged with fog and soot. Manufactories with their blackened bricks, their naked fronts, their windows destitute of shutters, and resembling huge and cheap penitentiaries, succeed each other in rows. … One of these buildings is a rectangle of six stories, in each of which are forty windows; it is there that, lit up by gas, amid the deafening noise of looms, thousands of workpeople, cabined, classified, immovable, mechanically drive their machines every day from morning to night; can any form of existence be more opposed to, and at variance with, the natural instincts of man? About six o'clock a bustling, noisy crowd pours from the mills into the streets; men, women, and children flock along in the open air; their clothes are filthy; many of the children are bare-footed, the faces of all are pinched and gloomy; several halt at the gin-palaces; the others scatter and hasten towards their hovels. …

… The life of one of the heads of these manufacturing or commercial houses may be likened to that of a minor prince. … they have to control and satisfy a host of workpeople; they have the power to become the benefactors of thousands of men; they are the generals and governors of human industry. … They despatch agents to examine particular districts of the globe; they discover outlets for commerce and markets for purchases in Japan, China, Australia, Egypt, and New Zealand …

paragraphs: The Utopians' mode of thought has for a long time governed the socialist ideas of the nineteenth century, and still governs some of them. … To all these Socialism is the expression of absolute truth, reason, and justice, and has only to be discovered to conquer all the world by virtue of its own power. And as absolute truth is independent of time, space, and of the historical development of man, it is a mere accident when and where it is discovered. …

These two great discoveries, the materialistic conception of history and the revelation of the secret of capitalistic production through surplus-value, we owe to Marx. With these discoveries Socialism became a science. …

The materialist conception of history starts from the proposition that the production of the means to support human life and, next to production, the exchange of things produced, is the basis of all social structure; that in every society that has appeared in history, the manner in which wealth is distributed and society divided into classes or orders, is dependent upon what is produced, how it is produced, and how the products are exchanged. From this point of view the final causes of all social changes and political revolutions are to be sought, not in men's brains, not in man's better insight into eternal truth and justice, but in changes in the modes of production and exchange. They are to be sought, not in the philosophy, but in the economics of each particular epoch.

paragraphs: Revolutions of 1848.—Revolutions had begun in Switzerland as early as 1847, in Sicily in January, 1848. The French revolution was not the first, but by its example it incited a general movement of democratic and nationalist insurrections. The governments, as yet inexperienced in the art of repression, seized with a mystical fear of revolution, a mysterious and incalculable force, lost heart and hardly resisted. Except in the extreme West (England, Spain, and Portugal), Sweden, Norway, and Russia, the movement was produced all over Europe. In Belgium, Holland, and Denmark it took the peaceful form of an electoral or constitutional reform. It was an internal revolution in France (February), in Austria and Prussia (March), in Germany, and in central Italy. It took the form of a nationalist movement, resulting in war, in northern Italy, Schleswig-Holstein, and Hungary. …

The Restorations (1849).—Austria, the power most shaken by the revolution of '48, set the example of military reaction. … The restoration was begun by Austria in October, 1848; the King of Prussia followed the example in Prussia in December. …

In Germany the conflict between the democrats and the governments turned into insurrection. The King of Prussia accomplished the restoration by means of his armies in Baden and in Saxony; the Frankfort Parliament dispersed. … Austria, threatened with a renewed invasion by the Hungarians, appealed to the Tsar; and it was a Russian army that conquered Hungary.

paragraphs: The natural and physical advantages of England for manufacturing industry are probably superior to those of every other country on the globe. …

Three things may be regarded as of primary importance for the successful prosecution of manufactures, namely, water-power, fuel, and iron. Wherever these exist in combination, and where they are abundant and cheap, machinery may be manufactured and put in motion at small cost …

Not less important for manufactures than the copious supply of good water, is the great abundance of coal found in the very same district. … It is superfluous to remark that this mineral fuel animates the thousand arms of the steam-engine, and furnishes the most powerful agent in all chemical and mechanical operations. …

To the above natural advantages, we must add, the acquired advantage of a canal communication, which ramifies itself through all the populous parts of this county* … The canals, having been accomplished by individual enterprise, not by national funds, were constructed to supply a want already existing … The recent introduction of railways will have a great effect in making the operations of trade more intensely active, and perfecting the division of labour, already carried to so high a point. …

The political and moral advantages of this country, as a seat of manufactures, are not less remarkable than its physical advantages. The arts are the daughters of peace and liberty. In no country have these blessings been enjoyed in so high a degree, or for so long a continuance, as in England. Under the reign of just laws, personal liberty and property have been secure; mercantile enterprise has been allowed to reap its reward; capital has accumulated in safety …

paragraphs: … under the existing conditions of the world, the result of general free trade would not be a universal republic, but, on the contrary, a universal subjection of the less advanced nations to the supremacy of the predominant manufacturing, commercial, and naval power … The system of protection, inasmuch as it forms the only means of placing those nations which are far behind in civilisation on equal terms with the one predominating nation (which, however, never received at the hands of Nature a perpetual right to a monopoly of manufacture, but which merely gained an advance over others in point of time), the system of protection regarded from this point of view appears to be the most efficient means of furthering the final union of nations, and hence also of promoting true freedom of trade. …

The advance which England has made in manufactures, navigation, and commerce, need therefore not discourage any other nation which is fitted for manufacturing production … But above all things we must have enough national spirit at once to plant and protect the tree, which will yield its first richest fruits only to future generations. We must first gain possession of the home market of our own nation, at least as respects articles of general necessity … This is especially the task which the German commercial union has to solve, if the German nation is not to remain far behind the French and North Americans, nay, far behind even the Russians. …

paragraphs: The Census of Ireland, in 1841, gave a population of 8,175,125. At the usual rate of increase, there must have been, in 1846, when the Famine commenced,* at least eight and a half millions; at the same rate of increase, there ought to have been, in 1851 (according to the estimate of the Census Commissioners), 9,018,799. But in that year, after five seasons of artificial famine, there were found alive only 6,552,385—a deficit of about two millions and a half. …

Further, I have called it an artificial famine: that is to say, it was a famine which desolated a rich and fertile island, that produced every year abundance and superabundance to sustain all her people and many more. The English,** indeed, call that famine a "dispensation of Providence;" and ascribe it entirely to the blight of the potatoes. But potatoes failed in like manner all over Europe; yet there was no famine save in Ireland. The British account of the matter, then, is first, a fraud—second, a blasphemy. The Almighty, indeed, sent the potato blight, but the English created the famine. …

… the benevolent contributions of Americans and other foreigners were turned aside from their destined objects—not, let us say, in order that none should be saved alive, but that no interference should be made with the principles of political economy.

paragraphs: Perhaps the best way to describe the new towns and their form of government would be to say that so far from breaking or checking the power of circumstances over men's lives, they symbolised the absolute dependence and helplessness of the mass of the people living in them. They were not so much towns as barracks: not the refuge of a civilisation but the barracks of an industry. … these towns reflected the violent enterprise of an hour, the single passion that had thrown street on street in a frantic monotony of disorder. … they represented nothing but the avarice of the jerry-builder catering for the avarice of the capitalist. …

And these towns were precisely what they looked. They were settlements of great masses of people collected in a particular place because their fingers or their muscles were needed on the brink of a stream here or at the mouth of a furnace there. These people were not citizens of this or that town, but hands of this or that master. Often the houses where they lived, and the shops where they bought their food, were supplied by their employers.

12. No assembly of men can give existence to a nation. An attempt of this kind ought even to be ranked among the most memorable acts of folly …
P8.attribution: Joseph de Maistre, Catholic writer and diplomat for the king of Sardinia, Essay on the Generative Principle of Political Constitutions, written in 1809 and published in 1814
P8.translation: English translation, Essay on the Generative Principle of Political Constitutions (Boston: Little and Brown, 1847), preface, pp. xi–xvii; adapted

We shall attempt to publish our papers without asking for the authorisation which is imposed upon us. The government has to-day lost the character which commands obedience. … while awaiting the regular action of the chambers, they have invited a Frenchman who has never fought except for France, Monsieur, the Duke of Orleans, to exercise the functions of lieutenant-general of the kingdom. …

The Duke of Orleans is devoted to the national and constitutional cause; he has always defended its interests and professed its principles. He will respect our rights, for he will hold his from us. We shall assure ourselves by laws all the necessary guarantees in order to render liberty strong and durable: … The jury for press offences; Legally organized responsibility of ministers …

paragraphs: Sire,— We working men of St. Petersburg, our wives and children, and our parents, helpless, aged men and women, have come to you, O Tsar, in quest of justice and protection. We have been beggared, oppressed, over-burdened with excessive toil, treated with contumely. … Therefore, we have left work, and informed our employers that we shall not resume it until they have fulfilled our demands. …

… O Emperor, there are more than three hundred thousand of us here, yet we are all of us human beings only in appearance and outwardly, while in reality we are deemed devoid of a single human right, even that of speaking, thinking, and meeting to talk over our needs, and of taking measures to better our condition. …

… Deliver them from the intolerable oppression of the bureaucracy. Demolish the wall between yourself and the people, and let them govern the country in conjunction with yourself. … Let all be free to elect whom they will, and for this purpose let the elections to the Constituent Assembly be organized on the principle of universal suffrage. This is our principal request, on which everything else depends. …

… In the first section are those which are directed against the ignorance and disfranchisement of the Russian people. They include—(1) Freedom and inviolability of the person, liberty of speech, of the press, of association, of conscience in matters of religion, and separation of Church and State. (2) General and obligatory education by the State. … The third section comprises measures against the crushing of labour by capital. … (3) An eight-hours working day and the limitation of overtime. …
P10.attribution: Petition of the workers of St. Petersburg, written by Father Georgy Gapon, a Russian Orthodox priest who led a workers' association, and carried in a march to the Winter Palace on January 22, 1905
P10.translation: English translation in Father George Gapon, The Story of My Life (New York: E. P. Dutton, 1906), appendix, pp. 257–261; adapted

paragraphs: That your honourable House, as at present constituted, has not been elected by, and acts irresponsibly of, the people; and hitherto has only represented parties, and benefitted the few, regardless of the miseries, grievances, and petitions of the many. …

That your petitioners instance, in proof of their assertion, that your honourable House has not been elected by the people; that the population of Great Britain and Ireland is at the present time about twenty-six millions of persons; and that yet, out of this number, little more than nine hundred thousand have been permitted to vote in the recent election of representatives to make laws to govern the whole. …

That your petitioners complain that the hours of labour, particularly of the factory workers, are protracted beyond the limits of human endurance, and that the wages earned, after unnatural application to toil in heated and unhealthy workshops, are inadequate to sustain the bodily strength …

That your petitioners, deeply deplore the existence of any kind of monopoly in this nation, and whilst they unequivocally condemn the levying of any tax upon the necessaries of life, and upon those articles principally required by the labouring classes, they are also sensible that the abolition of any one monopoly will never unshackle labour from its misery until the people possess that power under which all monopoly and oppression must cease …

That your petitioners, therefore, … demand that your honourable House … do immediately, without alteration, deduction, or addition, pass into a law the document entitled 'The People's Charter,' which embraces the representation of male adults, vote by ballot, annual Parliaments, no property qualification, payment of Members, and equal electoral districts.
P11.attribution: National petition of the Chartists to the House of Commons, presented May 2, 1842, with more than three million signatures
P11.translation: Text from Hansard's Parliamentary Debates, 3rd series, vol. 62, House of Commons, May 2, 1842 (UK Parliament, Historic Hansard); adapted

a rule that members of Parliament must own a certain amount of property

paragraphs: … it is a personal injustice to withhold from any one, unless for the prevention of greater evils, the ordinary privilege of having his voice reckoned in the disposal of affairs in which he has the same interest as other people. If he is compelled to pay, if he may be compelled to fight, if he is required implicitly to obey, he should be legally entitled to be told what for; to have his consent asked, and his opinion counted at its worth, though not at more than its worth. There ought to be no pariahs in a full-grown and civilized nation; no persons disqualified, except through their own default. …

There are, however, certain exclusions, required by positive reasons, which do not conflict with this principle … I regard it as wholly inadmissible that any person should participate in the suffrage, without being able to read, write, and, I will add, perform the common operations of arithmetic. …

In the preceding argument for universal, but graduated suffrage, I have taken no account of difference of sex. I consider it to be as entirely irrelevant to political rights, as difference in height, or in the colour of the hair. All human beings have the same interest in good government; the welfare of all is alike affected by it, and they have equal need of a voice in it to secure their share of its benefits.
P12.attribution: John Stuart Mill, English philosopher and economist, Considerations on Representative Government, 1861
P12.translation: Text from John Stuart Mill, Considerations on Representative Government (London: Parker, Son, and Bourn, 1861), pp. 166–167, 182–183; adapted

paragraphs: It is the characteristic of privilege and of every privileged position to kill the mind and heart of men. The privileged man, whether politically or economically, is a man depraved in mind and heart. …

But that which is true of scientific academies is also true of all constituent and legislative assemblies, even those chosen by universal suffrage. In the latter case they may renew their composition, it is true, but this does not prevent the formation in a few years' time of a body of politicians, privileged in fact though not in law, who, devoting themselves exclusively to the direction of the public affairs of a country, finally form a sort of political aristocracy or oligarchy. …

Does it follow that I reject all authority? Far from me such a thought. In the matter of boots I refer to the authority of the bootmakers; concerning houses, canals, or railroads I consult that of the architect or engineer. … But I allow neither the bootmaker nor the architect nor the savant to impose his authority upon me. …
… Each directs and is directed in his turn. Therefore there is no fixed and constant authority, but a continual exchange of mutual, temporary, and, above all, voluntary authority and subordination.
P13.attribution: Mikhail Bakunin, Russian revolutionary who lived in exile in western Europe, God and the State, written in 1871 and published after his death in 1882
P13.translation: English translation by Benjamin R. Tucker, God and the State, 8th edition (New York: Benj. R. Tucker, 1895), pp. 19–20; adapted

paragraphs: … The militancy of men, through all the centuries, has drenched the world with blood, and for these deeds of horror and destruction men have been rewarded with monuments, with great songs and epics. The militancy of women has harmed no human life save the lives of those who fought the battle of righteousness. …

By this time the Labour Party, of which I was still a member, had returned Mr. Keir Hardie to Parliament, and we decided that the first step in a campaign of action was to make the Labour Party responsible for a new suffrage bill. …

It was in October, 1903, that I invited a number of women to my house in Nelson street, Manchester, for purposes of organisation. We voted to call our new society the Women's Social and Political Union, partly to emphasise its democracy, and partly to define its object as political rather than propagandist. We resolved to limit our membership exclusively to women, to keep ourselves absolutely free from any party affiliation, and to be satisfied with nothing but action on our question. Deeds, not words, was to be our permanent motto.

To such a pass had the women's suffrage cause come in my country that the old leaders, who had done such fine educational work in the past, were now seemingly content with expressions of sympathy and regret on the part of hypocritical politicians. …
P14.attribution: Emmeline Pankhurst, English campaigner for women's right to vote, My Own Story, 1914
P14.translation: Text from Emmeline Pankhurst, My Own Story (London: Eveleigh Nash, 1914), foreword and pp. 37–38; adapted

fighting or aggressive action for a cause

paragraphs: … We must not delay. Upon the speedy provision of elementary education depends our industrial prosperity. It is of no use trying to give technical teaching to our artizans without elementary education; uneducated labourers—and many of our labourers are utterly uneducated—are, for the most part, unskilled labourers, and if we leave our work-folk any longer unskilled, notwithstanding their strong sinews and determined energy, they will become overmatched in the competition of the world.

Upon this speedy provision depends also, I fully believe, the good, the safe working of our constitutional system. To its honour, Parliament has lately decided that England shall in future be governed by popular government. I am one of those who would not wait until the people were educated before I would trust them with political power. If we had thus waited we might have waited long for education; but now that we have given them political power we must not wait any longer to give them education. There are questions demanding answers, problems which must be solved, which ignorant constituencies are ill-fitted to solve.

Upon this speedy provision of education depends also our national power. … if we are to hold our position among … the nations of the world we must make up the smallness of our numbers by increasing the intellectual force of the individual.
P15.attribution: William E. Forster, Liberal government minister in charge of education, speech in the House of Commons introducing the Elementary Education Bill, February 17, 1870

practice.stem: Which of the following best describes Baines's main argument?

options.A: England led in manufacturing because of its resources, its transport, and its secure laws.
options.B: England led in manufacturing because its government owned the mines, canals, and mills.
options.C: England led in manufacturing because its guilds trained more skilled workers than other countries.
options.D: England led in manufacturing because its growing population created a larger market for cotton cloth.

practice.explanation: Baines names three kinds of advantages. Some came from nature: water power, coal, and iron close together. Some were built: canals and new railways. Some came from government: "just laws," secure property, and safe money for business. Together, he says, they explain England's lead.

whyNot.B: Baines says the canals were built "by individual enterprise, not by national funds." British mines and mills were private businesses too.
whyNot.C: Guilds had lost most of their power in England by the 1700s. Baines credits water, coal, iron, canals, railways, and secure property instead.
whyNot.D: A growing population did help British industry. But Baines does not give it as a reason here. He credits England's resources, transport, and laws for its lead.

practice.hint: Baines sorts England's advantages into a few kinds. What are they?

practice.stem: Baines notes that England's canals were built "by individual enterprise, not by national funds." In contrast, industrialization in many continental European states after 1815 was more often

options.A: backed by governments that built or helped pay for railways
options.B: slowed by laws that banned private companies from building railways
options.C: led by craft guilds that owned and ran the new factories
options.D: led by peasant cooperatives that pooled village savings to build factories

practice.explanation: In Britain, private businessmen did most of the work of industrializing. In France, Belgium, and the German states, governments did more. They built or backed railways, set tariffs, and supported banks and technical schools.

whyNot.B: Governments on the continent built their own lines, but they also helped private railway companies. France's railway law of 1842, for example, joined state and private building.
whyNot.C: Guilds had little to do with the new factories, and many states weakened or abolished them in the 1800s. Factories were owned by private businessmen, sometimes with state help.
whyNot.D: Farm cooperatives spread later in the 1800s. They mostly ran dairies and village credit banks, not railways or factories. On the continent, states, banks, and private investors paid for industry.

practice.hint: Who paid for transport in Britain, according to Baines? Was it the same on the continent?

practice.stem: Baines's claim about England's "political and moral advantages" is best supported by which of the following?

options.A: Britain's kings ruled without Parliament for most of the 1700s, which kept taxes low for manufacturers.
options.B: Britain's Parliament, which included merchants and manufacturers, passed laws protecting property.
options.C: Britain's Reform Act of 1832 gave the vote to most adult men, including factory workers.
options.D: Britain's Parliament passed the Corn Laws to keep bread cheap for factory workers.

practice.explanation: Baines says that in England "personal liberty and property have been secure" and "capital has accumulated in safety." Britain's Parliament included men who made money from trade and industry. It passed laws that protected property and helped trade grow.

whyNot.A: Parliament met every year after 1689. Britain's kings did not rule without it.
whyNot.C: The Reform Act of 1832 gave the vote mainly to middle-class men. Most working men still could not vote, as the Chartists complained a few years later.
whyNot.D: The Corn Laws taxed grain brought in from abroad. They kept bread prices high and helped landowners, and manufacturers such as Richard Cobden fought to repeal them.

practice.hint: Baines praises "just laws." Which choice describes British government accurately?

practice.stem: Which of the following best describes List's main argument?

options.A: Nations should adopt free trade right away so that a peaceful union of nations can form.
options.B: Germany should win colonies overseas before it tries to build its own industries.
options.C: Less developed nations should protect their industries with tariffs until they can compete.
options.D: Britain's lead in manufacturing is a permanent gift of nature that other nations cannot hope to match.

practice.explanation: List says free trade helps the nation that is already ahead. Nations that are behind, such as Germany, should tax imports to "plant and protect the tree" of their own industry.

whyNot.A: List says free trade can come only after nations reach the same level. Until then, he calls protection "the only means" for nations that are "far behind."
whyNot.B: List says Germany must "first gain possession of the home market of our own nation." Colonies are not his first step.
whyNot.D: List says Britain "never received at the hands of Nature a perpetual right to a monopoly of manufacture." It only got there first.

practice.hint: What does List want Germany to do with its "home market"?

practice.stem: Members of which group would have most strongly disagreed with List's argument?

options.A: German manufacturers facing British competition
options.B: British free traders such as Richard Cobden
options.C: Prussian officials who led the Zollverein
options.D: American supporters of protective tariffs

practice.explanation: Cobden and the Anti-Corn Law League believed free trade made every nation richer and more peaceful. List made fun of that view. He said Britain preached free trade only after protection had made it strong. It was like someone who "kicks away the ladder" after climbing up.

whyNot.A: German manufacturers wanted protection from cheaper British goods. They would have welcomed List's ideas.
whyNot.C: List hoped the Zollverein, the "German commercial union," would protect Germany's home market. Some Prussian officials wanted lower tariffs than List did. But they did not reject all protection, as Cobden did.
whyNot.D: List had lived in the United States and admired American tariffs that protected new industries. Their supporters agreed with him.

practice.hint: List attacks the "cosmopolitical doctrine of Adam Smith." Who in the 1840s followed Smith's ideas on trade?

practice.stem: List's ideas were most directly reflected in which of the following later developments?

options.A: Britain's repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846
options.B: Britain's repeal of the Navigation Acts in 1849
options.C: The Anglo-French free-trade treaty of 1860
options.D: The German Empire's protective tariff law of 1879

practice.explanation: List's book helped convince Germans that new industries needed protection. In 1879, during a long economic slump, Bismarck's German Empire put tariffs on imported factory goods and grain.

whyNot.A: Repealing the Corn Laws moved Britain toward free trade in grain. List wanted something different: tariffs that protect a nation's new industries until they can compete.
whyNot.B: Ending the Navigation Acts let foreign ships carry British trade. It was another step toward free trade.
whyNot.C: The Cobden-Chevalier Treaty of 1860 cut tariffs between Britain and France. It moved away from protection, not toward it.

practice.hint: Three of these choices lowered trade barriers. Which one raised them?

practice.stem: Williams's concerns are best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.A: The first industrial revolution, when cotton spinning was mechanized in British mills
options.B: The Continental System, when Napoleon tried to close European markets to British goods
options.C: Germany's economic decline after its defeat in a war against France
options.D: The second industrial revolution's new, science-based industries

practice.explanation: After about 1870, new industries such as chemicals, electricity, and steel grew. They depended on science and trained engineers. Germany had strong technical schools and research labs. It became a leader in these industries and challenged Britain.

whyNot.A: The mechanization of cotton spinning came in the late 1700s and early 1800s, and Britain led it. Williams writes in 1896 about chemicals, where Germany led.
whyNot.B: The Continental System lasted from 1806 to 1814. Williams describes German competition in the 1890s.
whyNot.C: Germany defeated France in 1870–1871 and grew rapidly afterward. Williams links the new German Empire to its industrial rise.

practice.hint: When did chemicals become a major industry, and which country led it?

practice.stem: Williams most likely wrote the book in order to

options.A: warn British leaders to improve technical education to meet German competition
options.B: persuade German manufacturers to sell more of their chemicals and steel in British markets
options.C: argue that Britain should adopt socialism so that its industries could compete with Germany's
options.D: show that Britain's lead in chemicals and steel was safe from German and American rivals

practice.explanation: Williams dedicated his book to British factory owners and merchants. He warns them that Britain is losing its lead. He points to Germany's science and technical schools as one reason for German success.

whyNot.B: Williams is British and calls Germany "a more formidable rival." He wants British firms to win back markets from German ones, not help them.
whyNot.C: Williams praises German schools, but he does not call for socialism. He wants Britain's own factory owners to compete better.
whyNot.D: Williams says the opposite. He writes, "The industrial glory of England is departing." He adds that Germany has "given us a sounder beating in Chemicals."

practice.hint: Who was the book written for, and what does Williams want them to notice?

practice.stem: Which of the following would best support Williams's explanation of Germany's industrial success?

options.A: Germany's rapidly growing population created a large home market for goods from its factories.
options.B: The Zollverein removed customs barriers between many of the German states.
options.C: German firms hired university-trained chemists to invent synthetic dyes and medicines.
options.D: German governments placed large orders with German firms for steel rails and weapons.

practice.explanation: Williams credits "the German Chemist" and the state's "Scientific and Technical Education." Companies such as BASF, Bayer, and Hoechst hired chemists trained at universities. These chemists invented new man-made dyes and drugs. By 1900 Germany made most of the world's synthetic dyes.

whyNot.A: A larger market could help industry grow. But it does not show the role of science and technical training that Williams stresses.
whyNot.B: The Zollverein helped trade among the German states. But it does not show the benefits of the education Williams praises.
whyNot.D: Government orders helped heavy industry. But Williams praises the German state for its schools, not for its orders.

practice.hint: What does Williams connect to Germany's success in chemicals?

practice.stem: Mitchel's argument is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.A: A British ban on emigration that kept starving Irish families from leaving the island
options.B: A war between Britain and France that cut off food shipments to Ireland
options.C: Government orders that kept Irish grain and cattle from being sold abroad
options.D: Britain's reluctance to interfere with free markets during the Irish famine

practice.explanation: Many British officials believed in laissez-faire, the idea that government should stay out of markets. Help for the hungry was slow and limited, and food was still shipped out of Ireland. Mitchel blames "the principles of political economy" for the deaths.

whyNot.A: Britain did not ban emigration. More than a million people left Ireland during and after the famine.
whyNot.B: Britain was at peace with France in the 1840s. The famine was caused by potato blight and made worse by policy, not by war.
whyNot.C: The government did not stop food from leaving Ireland. Grain, cattle, and butter were still shipped out during the famine.

practice.hint: Mitchel blames "the principles of political economy." What economic idea guided the British government in the 1840s?

practice.stem: A historian would most likely challenge which of the following claims in the passage?

options.A: That Ireland's population in 1851 was far lower than it had been ten years before, in 1841
options.B: That potato blight was the immediate cause of the crop failures
options.C: That Americans and other foreigners sent aid to Ireland during the famine
options.D: That potatoes failed in other parts of Europe without causing famine there

practice.explanation: Potato blight also struck the Scottish Highlands, Belgium, the Netherlands, and parts of the German states in the 1840s. This decade is known as the Hungry Forties. People went hungry and death rates rose there too. But no other place suffered as Ireland did.

whyNot.A: The census figures Mitchel cites are real: about 8.2 million people in 1841 and about 6.6 million in 1851. That is a drop of about 1.6 million. His larger "deficit" compares the 1851 count with the number the census officials had expected.
whyNot.B: Mitchel himself says "The Almighty, indeed, sent the potato blight." Historians agree that blight destroyed the crops.
whyNot.C: People in the United States and other countries did send money and food to Ireland, as Mitchel says.

practice.hint: Three choices are facts most historians accept. Which claim goes too far?

practice.stem: The famine Mitchel describes most directly contributed to which of the following in the second half of the 1800s?

options.A: The rapid growth of new factory towns in the west of Ireland
options.B: Mass emigration from Ireland to Britain and North America
options.C: The creation of a separate parliament for Ireland in Dublin
options.D: A return to rapid population growth as Irish couples married younger

practice.explanation: About a million people died during the famine years, and more than a million left Ireland. People kept leaving for decades, so Ireland's population kept falling. Irish communities grew in Liverpool, Glasgow, New York, Boston, and other cities.

whyNot.A: Western Ireland stayed rural and poor. Ireland's main industrial area was around Belfast in the northeast.
whyNot.C: Bills to give Ireland its own parliament, called Home Rule bills, failed in 1886 and 1893. Most of Ireland did not govern itself until 1922, when it became the Irish Free State.
whyNot.D: Ireland's population kept falling for decades after the famine. Many people married later in life, and many did not marry at all.

practice.hint: Where did many of the missing millions go?

practice.stem: Which of the following best describes a difference between the two sources?

options.A: The Hammonds rely on statistics about wages and prices, while Clapham relies on descriptions of how towns looked.
options.B: The Hammonds praise employers for providing housing, while Clapham blames employers for crowded towns.
options.C: The Hammonds argue that workers' lives improved after 1820, while Clapham argues that they grew steadily worse.
options.D: The Hammonds stress the misery of life in the towns, while Clapham stresses that wages bought more over time.

practice.explanation: The Hammonds judge the new towns by how people lived. They show ugly, crowded "barracks of an industry," where workers depended on their masters. Clapham judges by facts that can be measured, such as how much wages could buy. Historians call this the standard-of-living debate.

whyNot.A: This reverses the sources. Clapham calls for numbers and complains that social historians ignore "the work of statisticians on wages and prices."
whyNot.B: The Hammonds say employers supplied houses and shops. But they say it to show that workers were "hands of this or that master," not to praise employers.
whyNot.C: This reverses the sources. Clapham says that after 1820–1821, what wages could buy was "definitely greater." He calls the idea that "everything was getting worse" a "legend."

practice.hint: One source judges by how life felt and looked, the other by numbers. Which is which?

practice.stem: Clapham would most likely criticize the approach of the Hammonds in Source 1 because it

options.A: relies on descriptions rather than on wage and price figures
options.B: depends too heavily on government statistics about wages and hours
options.C: ignores the role of factory owners in building houses in the new towns
options.D: blames the workers themselves for the crowded, unhealthy towns

practice.explanation: Clapham complains that "the work of statisticians on wages and prices" is "constantly ignored by social historians." He says they repeat a "tradition" that life got worse. The Hammonds' passage makes its case with vivid description, not numbers.

whyNot.B: The Hammonds' passage gives no statistics at all. Clapham's complaint is that social historians ignore the numbers.
whyNot.C: The Hammonds do mention employers. Employers "supplied" houses and shops and stood behind the "jerry-builder."
whyNot.D: The Hammonds blame "the avarice of the jerry-builder" and of "the capitalist," not the workers.

practice.hint: What kind of evidence does Clapham say social historians leave out?

practice.stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence would best support Clapham's argument?

options.A: Reports of crowded cellars and frequent outbreaks of fever in Manchester in the 1840s
options.B: Testimony that young children worked long hours in coal mines in 1842
options.C: Records showing that prices of food and clothing fell faster than wages after 1820
options.D: Accounts of hunger in the countryside during the "Hungry '40s"

practice.explanation: What workers can buy depends on both their pay and the prices of goods. If prices fell faster than wages, a week's pay bought more. That is what Clapham means by the greater "purchasing power of wages."

whyNot.A: Reports of crowded, unhealthy housing fit the Hammonds' picture of the new towns. They do not support Clapham's claim about wages.
whyNot.B: Evidence of child labor in the mines shows hard working conditions. It does not show what wages could buy.
whyNot.D: Hunger in the 1840s shows hard times for some people. But Clapham writes about wages "in general," and these accounts do not measure what wages could buy.

practice.hint: What two kinds of numbers would show how much a week's pay could buy?

practice.stem: Source 1 is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.A: The entry of large numbers of middle-class wives into factory work
options.B: New laws that gave married women control over their own property and wages
options.C: The middle-class ideal of separate spheres for men and women
options.D: The Catholic Church's campaign to limit women's work outside the home

practice.explanation: Work moved out of homes into offices and factories. So middle-class families came to see the home as a separate, moral "sphere" run by women. Ellis says men face a "worldly" struggle in business. They come home "a wiser and a better man" because of their wives.

whyNot.A: Most factory women were working-class girls and young women. Middle-class wives were expected to stay at home.
whyNot.B: The Married Women's Property Acts came in 1870 and 1882, decades after Ellis wrote. Source 2 shows that in the 1850s a wife's earnings still belonged to her husband.
whyNot.D: Ellis was an English Protestant writer. Her ideas came from middle-class English culture, not from Catholic teaching.

practice.hint: Where does Ellis place men's work, and where does she place women's influence?

practice.stem: Which of the following best describes a difference between the two sources?

options.A: Ellis calls for married women to control their own wages, while Smith argues that women's place is in the home.
options.B: Ellis wants women to vote for members of Parliament, while Smith thinks women should stay out of politics.
options.C: Ellis describes the lives of working-class women, while Smith writes about the wives of rich landowners.
options.D: Ellis praises women's influence in the home, while Smith attacks laws that strip married women of their rights.

practice.explanation: Ellis accepts women's limited "sphere" and praises their moral power at home. Smith attacks the laws of her time. Under the law of coverture, a wife became part of her husband in law, and her earnings and the custody of her children belonged to him. Separate voting laws kept all women, even single women with property, from voting for Parliament.

whyNot.A: This reverses the sources. Smith is the one who wants married women to keep "their own earnings."
whyNot.B: Ellis does not mention voting. Smith points out that a woman "cannot vote" even if she has property, which she presents as unfair.
whyNot.C: Ellis writes about the wives of "men of business." Smith mentions "women of the labouring classes" whose earnings are taken.

practice.hint: Does each author accept or challenge women's position in her time?

practice.stem: The reform Smith calls for in the last paragraph of Source 2 was most directly addressed by which of the following?

options.A: The Married Women's Property Acts
options.B: The Ten Hours Act
options.C: The Mines and Collieries Act
options.D: The Second Reform Act

practice.explanation: In the last paragraph, Smith wants wives to be able to keep "their own earnings." Campaigns that Barbara Leigh Smith helped start led to the Married Women's Property Acts. The act of 1870 let wives keep their own earnings, and the act of 1882 let them own property in their own names.

whyNot.B: The Ten Hours Act of 1847 limited the working day of women and young people in textile mills. It did not change property law.
whyNot.C: The Mines Act of 1842 barred women and girls from working underground. It did not let wives keep their earnings.
whyNot.D: The Second Reform Act of 1867 gave the vote to many working men. Women still could not vote in parliamentary elections.

practice.hint: What does Smith want working wives to be able to keep?

practice.stem: Ashley's hope for "a good understanding between master and man, between wealth and poverty" was most likely intended to

options.A: assure Parliament that reform would strengthen social order
options.B: call on miners to form unions and strike for higher pay
options.C: urge the government to take over ownership of the coal mines
options.D: argue that working men should be given the right to vote

practice.explanation: Ashley is speaking to landowners and other men of property in Parliament. He says that ending "oppression" would bring back good feeling between classes. It would also protect "the permanent security of the empire."

whyNot.B: Ashley speaks to Parliament and asks "those who have the power" to act. He does not call on miners to strike.
whyNot.C: Ashley asks for a law to stop abuses. He does not propose that the state own the mines.
whyNot.D: Ashley was a Conservative who sought laws to protect workers, not votes for them. His goal here is a law about mines.

practice.hint: Who was Ashley speaking to, and what might worry them?

practice.stem: The testimony of Mr. Wood in the last paragraph most directly reflects which of the following beliefs common among reformers?

options.A: Women should have the same right as men to work underground.
options.B: Children learned useful skills by working beside their parents in the mines.
options.C: Women's proper role was to keep a comfortable home for their families.
options.D: Mining families should move to factory towns where wages were higher.

practice.explanation: Wood blames women's mine work for homes that are not "comfortable" and for husbands "driven to the alehouse." Like many middle-class reformers, he believed a woman's job was to keep the home.

whyNot.A: Wood argues that mine work harms women. He does not defend their right to do it.
whyNot.B: Wood says this work "shuts them out entirely from all useful and necessary knowledge."
whyNot.D: Wood does not mention factory towns. His concern is what mine work does to women's ability to run a home.

practice.hint: What does Wood say goes wrong at home when girls work in mines?

practice.stem: The law passed soon after this speech most directly

options.A: made mine owners pay miners who were hurt at work
options.B: gave miners the right to form trade unions for the first time
options.C: limited the working day of adult miners to eight hours
options.D: barred women, girls, and young boys from underground work

practice.explanation: The Mines Act of 1842 banned all women and girls, and boys under ten, from working underground. It was one of the first laws to limit the labor of women as well as children.

whyNot.A: The 1842 law did not make owners pay for injuries. The Workmen's Compensation Act of 1897 was the first law to make employers pay workers hurt on the job even when no one was to blame.
whyNot.B: Trade unions became legal in 1824–1825, when the Combination Acts were repealed. That was long before 1842.
whyNot.C: An eight-hour day for coal miners came only in 1908.

practice.hint: The speech focuses on young children and on women and girls underground. What did the new law do about them?

practice.stem: The ideas in the passage most directly express which of the following ideologies?

options.A: Liberalism
options.B: Utopian socialism
options.C: Anarchism
options.D: Conservatism

practice.explanation: De Maistre was a leading conservative. He believed that lasting governments and customs grow slowly out of history, religion, and the rule of kings. Reason and assemblies, he said, cannot invent a nation or a constitution.

whyNot.A: Liberals wanted elected assemblies to write constitutions and declare rights. De Maistre says, "The more is written, the weaker the constitution."
whyNot.B: Utopian socialists such as Robert Owen and Charles Fourier planned new communities from scratch. De Maistre says careful planning cannot create a lasting constitution.
whyNot.C: Anarchists wanted to abolish all government. De Maistre calls liberty "the gift of kings."

practice.hint: Does de Maistre trust kings and tradition, or written plans and assemblies?

practice.stem: De Maistre's claim that "No assembly of men can give existence to a nation" is best understood as a reaction against

options.A: the Congress of Vienna's plan to restore Europe's old ruling families
options.B: the Protestant reformers' challenge to the authority of the pope
options.C: French revolutionaries' efforts to remake France by written constitutions
options.D: Napoleon's agreement with the pope that restored the Catholic Church in France

practice.explanation: Between 1789 and 1799, French assemblies wrote several constitutions and declared new rights. De Maistre called such paper plans "folly." True constitutions, he said, come from God, history, and kings.

whyNot.A: De Maistre supported the return of legitimate kings, which the Congress of Vienna carried out in 1814–1815.
whyNot.B: The Reformation took place in the 1500s. De Maistre is answering the assemblies of the French Revolution, in his own lifetime.
whyNot.D: The Concordat of 1801 was an agreement between Napoleon and the pope, not a plan written by an assembly. De Maistre attacks assemblies that write constitutions.

practice.hint: What did French assemblies do again and again after 1789?

practice.stem: Which of the following figures acted most in keeping with de Maistre's ideas?

options.A: John Stuart Mill
options.B: Prince Metternich
options.C: Pierre-Joseph Proudhon
options.D: Lajos Kossuth

practice.explanation: Metternich was Austria's foreign minister from 1809 and its chancellor until 1848. He defended kings and the order set up in 1815. Through the Concert of Europe, he worked to crush liberal and nationalist revolutions.

whyNot.A: Mill was a liberal. He wanted more people to vote, and he wanted elected government to protect each person's freedom.
whyNot.C: Proudhon was a French anarchist. He wanted free groups of workers to take the place of government.
whyNot.D: Kossuth led Hungary's revolt against Austria's Habsburg rulers in 1848–1849. He was a liberal and a nationalist.

practice.hint: Which figure spent his career defending kings against revolution?

practice.stem: The journalists in Source 1 were most directly protesting against which of the following?

options.A: Louis XVIII's Constitutional Charter of 1814
options.B: Napoleon I's censorship of the French press
options.C: Louis-Philippe's September Laws on the press
options.D: Charles X's decrees suspending press freedom

practice.explanation: On July 25, 1830, King Charles X issued the July Ordinances. They suspended freedom of the press, broke up the newly elected Chamber of Deputies, and changed the election rules. Paris journalists refused to obey, and three days of street fighting followed.

whyNot.A: The Charter of 1814 let the French publish their opinions, within the law. The journalists were not protesting against it. They say the king's new orders broke the law.
whyNot.B: Napoleon I censored newspapers while he ruled France. But his rule ended in 1815, fifteen years before this protest.
whyNot.C: Louis-Philippe became king only after the July Revolution. His September Laws of 1835 limited the press five years after this protest.

practice.hint: Which ruler governed France in July 1830, and what had he just ordered?

practice.stem: The government that grew out of the events described in Source 2 is best described as

options.A: a democratic republic with universal male suffrage
options.B: a constitutional monarchy with the vote limited to the wealthy
options.C: an absolute monarchy restored with the help of foreign armies
options.D: an empire ruled by Napoleon's nephew, Louis Napoleon

practice.explanation: The deputies made the Duke of Orleans king, as Louis-Philippe. His July Monarchy had a revised charter and a freer press. But only men who paid high taxes could vote, and they were a small share of the country's men.

whyNot.A: In 1830 the deputies chose a new king, not a republic. France's Second Republic, which let all adult men vote, began in 1848.
whyNot.C: Foreign armies helped restore the Bourbon kings in 1814–1815. In 1830 Parisians overthrew the Bourbon king.
whyNot.D: Napoleon's nephew, Louis Napoleon, did not make himself emperor until 1852.

practice.hint: The deputies chose a duke to lead France. Who could vote under the king he became?

practice.stem: The events described in the sources most directly inspired which of the following in 1830?

options.A: The Belgian revolt against Dutch rule
options.B: The Decembrist revolt of army officers in Russia
options.C: The Greek war for independence from the Ottomans
options.D: The Frankfurt Parliament

practice.explanation: News of the July Revolution set off a revolt in Brussels in August 1830. The Belgians broke away from the Kingdom of the Netherlands, which the Congress of Vienna had created. Later the great powers recognized Belgium as an independent country.

whyNot.B: The Decembrist revolt took place in December 1825, five years earlier.
whyNot.C: The Greek war for independence began in 1821. By 1830 the great powers had recognized Greek independence.
whyNot.D: The Frankfurt Parliament met in 1848–1849.

practice.hint: Which of these events happened in 1830?

practice.stem: The petition is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.A: State-backed industrial growth that created a large, powerless factory workforce
options.B: The emancipation of the serfs, which Tsar Alexander II had just announced to the empire
options.C: Russia's victories over Japan, which had strengthened the tsar's government at home
options.D: The Bolshevik takeover of the Russian government in the capital, Petrograd

practice.explanation: In the 1890s, finance minister Sergei Witte pushed Russian industry ahead with state railways, tariffs, and foreign loans. Factories grew in cities like St. Petersburg. But workers could not legally strike or form independent trade unions, and they had no say in government. The government allowed only a few workers' groups that it watched closely, such as Gapon's.

whyNot.B: Alexander II freed the serfs in 1861, more than forty years before this petition.
whyNot.C: Russia was losing its war with Japan (1904–1905). The defeats weakened the tsar's government.
whyNot.D: The Bolsheviks took power in 1917, twelve years later.

practice.hint: Who were the petitioners, and how had Russia's economy been changing?

practice.stem: The events that followed this petition led most directly to which of the following later in 1905?

options.A: The emancipation of the serfs
options.B: The abdication of Nicholas II
options.C: The assassination of Alexander II
options.D: The October Manifesto

practice.explanation: Troops fired on the marchers on Bloody Sunday, January 22, 1905. Strikes and revolts spread across Russia. In October, Nicholas II issued the October Manifesto. It promised basic freedoms and an elected lawmaking body, the Duma.

whyNot.A: The serfs were freed in 1861.
whyNot.B: Nicholas II gave up the throne in March 1917, during the First World War.
whyNot.C: A bomb thrown by revolutionaries killed Alexander II in 1881. That was 24 years earlier.

practice.hint: Only one choice happened in 1905. What did the tsar promise that year?

practice.stem: The demands in the petition are most similar to those of which earlier movement?

options.A: The Burschenschaften in the German states
options.B: The Anti-Corn Law League in Britain
options.C: The Chartists in Britain
options.D: The utopian socialist communities of Robert Owen

practice.explanation: Like the Gapon petition, the Chartist petitions came from working people. They blamed their hard lives on their lack of political power. Both asked for elections by universal suffrage (for the Chartists, all men) as the key reform.

whyNot.A: The Burschenschaften were university student clubs that worked for German unity. They were not workers asking for the vote.
whyNot.B: The Anti-Corn Law League was led by manufacturers and asked for free trade in grain, not for votes for all.
whyNot.D: Owen tried to change society by building model communities. He did not petition for elections or for the vote for all.

practice.hint: Find the movement in which workers petitioned for the vote as the answer to their hardships.

practice.stem: Which of the following best describes the main argument of the petition?

options.A: Working people suffer because factory owners have too little influence in the House of Commons.
options.B: Working people suffer because they lack political power, which the Charter would give them.
options.C: Working people suffer because Parliament has grown too strong and the monarch should rule alone.
options.D: Working people suffer because of new machines, which the House of Commons should ban.

practice.explanation: The Chartists blamed long hours, low wages, and high taxes on laws made by a Parliament that only "little more than nine hundred thousand" men had elected. Their remedy was the six points of the People's Charter.

whyNot.A: The petition says the House has "benefitted the few." It wants working men represented, not more power for factory owners.
whyNot.C: The petition asks the House to pass the People's Charter. It does not ask for rule by the monarch.
whyNot.D: The petition attacks "monopoly" and laws made by "the few," not machines. It demands the Charter, not a ban on machines.

practice.hint: What do the petitioners want Parliament to pass?

practice.stem: The petitioners' statement that "the abolition of any one monopoly will never unshackle labour" was most likely aimed at the arguments of which of the following?

options.A: Supporters of the New Poor Law
options.B: The Anti-Corn Law League
options.C: Robert Owen's cooperative movement
options.D: Opponents of the Factory Acts

practice.explanation: The Anti-Corn Law League called the tax on grain a monopoly. It told workers that ending the tax would bring cheap bread and better times. The Chartists answered that only political power for working people would end their misery.

whyNot.A: Supporters of the New Poor Law of 1834 defended workhouses. They did not claim that ending one monopoly would free labor.
whyNot.C: Owen's followers wanted workers to share ownership in cooperatives. They did not ask for the repeal of a single tax.
whyNot.D: Opponents of the Factory Acts wanted to keep hours unregulated. They did not promise that ending a monopoly would help workers.

practice.hint: Which group called the Corn Laws a "monopoly" and promised that repeal would help workers?

practice.stem: The complaint in the third paragraph was most directly addressed by which of the following later laws?

options.A: The Second Reform Act
options.B: The Public Health Act
options.C: The Ten Hours Act
options.D: The Married Women's Property Act

practice.explanation: The Ten Hours Act of 1847 limited women and young people in textile mills to ten hours of work a day. Reformers expected men's hours to fall too, because mills needed these workers. Some owners got around the law by using shifts. So an act of 1850 set fixed hours for women and young workers. In practice, this set the working day in most mills.

whyNot.A: The Second Reform Act of 1867 widened the vote. It did not limit working hours.
whyNot.B: The Public Health Act of 1848 dealt with drains, water, and sanitation in towns, not factory hours.
whyNot.D: The Married Women's Property Act of 1870 let wives keep their earnings. It did not shorten the working day.

practice.hint: The third paragraph is about "the hours of labour" in factories. Which law dealt with hours?

practice.stem: Mill's argument is best described as support for

options.A: a broad vote for both sexes, limited to people who can read, write, and do arithmetic
options.B: universal male suffrage without any test of literacy or property
options.C: a vote limited to men who own land, since landowners have the most at stake
options.D: replacing elected assemblies with government by a council of trained scientific experts

practice.explanation: Mill believed nearly everyone, including women, deserved a voice in government. But he wanted voters to be able to read, write, and do arithmetic. He also favored "graduated" suffrage, which would give extra votes to the well educated.

whyNot.B: Mill says it is "wholly inadmissible" for someone who cannot read, write, and do arithmetic to vote. He also includes women.
whyNot.C: Mill says there "ought to be no pariahs" and calls exclusion "a personal injustice." He does not tie the vote to land.
whyNot.D: Mill is writing about how to set up "representative government." He wants more people to vote, not fewer elections.

practice.hint: Look for the choice that matches both Mill's "no pariahs" and his literacy rule.

practice.stem: Mill's views most clearly illustrate which of the following?

options.A: Conservatives defended monarchy as a gift of God and tradition.
options.B: Socialists called for the state to own land and factories.
options.C: Anarchists rejected elected assemblies as a new aristocracy.
options.D: Liberals disagreed about how far the right to vote should be extended.

practice.explanation: In the 1800s, liberals agreed on rights and representative government. But they disagreed about who should vote. Mill wanted a broad vote that included women. He also wanted a reading and writing test and extra votes for the educated.

whyNot.A: De Maistre and other conservatives defended kings and tradition. Mill argues for elected, representative government.
whyNot.B: Mill does not call for state ownership. His topic is who should vote.
whyNot.C: Bakunin and other anarchists distrusted all assemblies. Mill wants assemblies elected by a wide body of voters.

practice.hint: Mill supports representative government but sets conditions on voting. Which group argued about such conditions?

practice.stem: The ideas in Mill's last paragraph were most directly advanced later by which of the following?

options.A: The Anti-Corn Law League of Manchester
options.B: The Women's Social and Political Union
options.C: The Chartist movement for the People's Charter
options.D: The Ten Hours movement for factory reform

practice.explanation: Mill argued that sex is as "irrelevant to political rights" as height. In 1867 he asked Parliament to give women the vote and lost. Later groups such as the Women's Social and Political Union, founded in 1903, kept up the fight.

whyNot.A: The Anti-Corn Law League campaigned for free trade in grain from 1838 to 1846, before Mill's book.
whyNot.C: The Chartists campaigned from 1838 to about 1848, and they asked for votes for men only.
whyNot.D: The Ten Hours movement won its law in 1847. It sought shorter working hours, not votes for women.

practice.hint: Which group came after 1861 and worked for women's votes?

practice.stem: The ideas in the passage are most closely associated with which of the following?

options.A: Marxian socialism
options.B: Liberalism
options.C: Anarchism
options.D: Conservatism

practice.explanation: Anarchists such as Bakunin thought all government was harmful. They wanted to replace it with "voluntary" cooperation, so that no one would hold power over others for long.

whyNot.A: Marx's followers wanted workers to win power through parties and elections, or through revolution. Bakunin distrusts every fixed authority, even elected ones.
whyNot.B: Liberals trusted elected assemblies to protect rights. Bakunin says even assemblies that everyone votes for become "a sort of political aristocracy."
whyNot.D: Conservatives defended kings, nobles, and the Church. Bakunin attacks privilege of every kind.

practice.hint: Bakunin accepts only one kind of authority. What kind is it?

practice.stem: Bakunin's view of assemblies "chosen by universal suffrage" contrasts most strongly with the views of which of the following?

options.A: Georges Sorel
options.B: Pierre-Joseph Proudhon
options.C: The Chartists
options.D: Joseph de Maistre

practice.explanation: The Chartists believed that a Parliament elected by all men would stop serving only the rich. Bakunin said that even such an assembly would turn into a new group of privileged politicians.

whyNot.A: Sorel, a French syndicalist, also distrusted parliaments. He urged workers to act directly through strikes.
whyNot.B: Proudhon, a French anarchist, also opposed government power. He wanted people to form free groups instead.
whyNot.D: De Maistre also distrusted elected assemblies, though for the opposite reason: he wanted rule by kings.

practice.hint: Three choices also distrusted parliaments. Which group put its hope in elections?

practice.stem: Ideas like Bakunin's contributed most directly to which development in Russia?

options.A: Alexander II's decision to free the serfs from their lords in 1861
options.B: Revolutionary groups, one of which killed Tsar Alexander II in 1881
options.C: Nicholas II's creation of an elected assembly, the Duma, in 1905
options.D: Sergei Witte's program of state-funded railways and factories in the 1890s

practice.explanation: Russian radicals, inspired by Bakunin and others, formed secret groups. One of them, the People's Will, killed Alexander II with a bomb in 1881. His son, the next tsar, answered with harsh crackdowns.

whyNot.A: The emancipation was a reform from above by the tsar, meant to head off revolt from below.
whyNot.C: Nicholas II set up the Duma to calm the revolution of 1905. Bakunin's followers distrusted assemblies like it.
whyNot.D: Witte's program was a state plan to make Russia strong. Anarchists opposed the state.

practice.hint: Which choice describes people working against the tsar's government?

practice.stem: Pankhurst most likely wrote the first paragraph in order to

options.A: praise the soldiers of 1914 for the glory they would soon win in the war
options.B: defend militant tactics by comparing them with men's far deadlier violence
options.C: argue that women should stay out of the nation's public life
options.D: explain why the women's union had decided to join the Labour Party

practice.explanation: Suffragettes broke windows, set fires, and went on hunger strikes. Critics called them violent. Pankhurst answers that women's militancy "has harmed no human life" except their own. Men's wars, by contrast, have killed millions.

whyNot.A: Pankhurst says men's militancy has "drenched the world with blood." She is not praising it.
whyNot.C: Pankhurst founded a political union to win the vote for women. She wanted women in public life.
whyNot.D: The union decided "to keep ourselves absolutely free from any party affiliation."

practice.hint: Pankhurst contrasts two kinds of "militancy." Why?

practice.stem: The founding of the Women's Social and Political Union is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.A: Decades of failed petitions and bills for women's suffrage
options.B: A recent law granting universal male suffrage in Britain
options.C: The election of women to the House of Commons a few years earlier
options.D: A recent law that took away married women's right to keep their own earnings

practice.explanation: British women had sent petitions for the vote since the 1860s, and bills for women's suffrage kept failing. Pankhurst says the old leaders were "content with expressions of sympathy" from politicians. In 1903 she founded the WSPU with the motto "Deeds, not words."

whyNot.B: Britain did not give the vote to nearly all adult men until 1918. In 1903 many working men still could not vote.
whyNot.C: Women could not be elected to the House of Commons until 1918, and the first woman took her seat in 1919.
whyNot.D: Parliament did not take that right away. The Married Women's Property Act of 1882 gave wives even more control of their property than the act of 1870. It was still in force in 1903.

practice.hint: Pankhurst complains about "the old leaders." What had they been doing, and how well had it worked?

practice.stem: The Labour Party mentioned in the second paragraph is best described as a party that

options.A: was formed by landowners who wanted to bring back the Corn Laws
options.B: was formed by free-trade liberals who wanted to limit the role of government
options.C: refused to take part in elections and called for a general strike instead
options.D: was formed by trade unions and socialist groups to represent workers

practice.explanation: Trade unions and socialist groups formed the Labour Representation Committee in 1900. One of those groups was the Independent Labour Party, which Pankhurst belonged to. The committee took the name Labour Party in 1906 and became one of the large parties that spoke for workers.

whyNot.A: Landowners who wanted tariffs on grain were mostly Conservatives. Labour grew out of the workers' movement.
whyNot.B: Free-trade liberals made up the Liberal Party. Labour wanted laws to help workers, not a smaller government.
whyNot.C: Labour ran candidates in elections. Pankhurst says it had "returned Mr. Keir Hardie to Parliament."

practice.hint: Keir Hardie was a former miner and union organizer. What kind of party would elect him?

practice.stem: Forster's statement that "Parliament has lately decided that England shall in future be governed by popular government" refers to which of the following?

options.A: The Reform Act that gave the vote to many working men in towns
options.B: The Reform Act that gave the vote to middle-class men in industrial towns
options.C: A law that gave women the right to vote
options.D: The repeal of the Corn Laws

practice.explanation: The Second Reform Act of 1867 roughly doubled the number of voters and gave the vote to many working men in towns. Forster argues that these new voters must now be educated.

whyNot.B: The First Reform Act of 1832 gave the vote to many middle-class men. Forster speaks of a decision made "lately," and it gave power to working men.
whyNot.C: Some women won the vote in 1918, and all adult women in 1928, long after Forster spoke.
whyNot.D: The repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846 was about the grain trade, not about who could vote.

practice.hint: Forster says Parliament has "given them political power." Who are "them"?

practice.stem: Which of the following best summarizes Forster's reasons for public education?

options.A: Religious unity, loyalty to the Church, and moral reform
options.B: Protecting children from dangerous work in factories and mines
options.C: Economic success, safe self-government, and national power
options.D: Preparing young men to serve as soldiers overseas

practice.explanation: Forster gives three reasons. Schools would help "our industrial prosperity," "the safe working of our constitutional system," and "our national power." Many governments at this time backed public schools for the same reasons.

whyNot.A: Forster's reasons in this passage are about industry, voting, and national strength. He does not mention the Church.
whyNot.B: Forster wants schooling so workers become skilled, not to keep children out of work.
whyNot.D: Forster speaks of "national power" and "intellectual force," not of training soldiers.

practice.hint: Forster starts three sentences with "Upon … depends." What depends on education?

practice.stem: Forster's concern that unskilled workers "will become overmatched in the competition of the world" most likely reflected

options.A: Britain's loss of most of its colonies in Asia and Africa to rivals
options.B: a fall in British trade after the repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846
options.C: growing industrial competition from Germany and the United States
options.D: competition from the factories built in Russia under Sergei Witte

practice.explanation: By 1870 Germany and the United States were building industry fast, and Prussia was known for its schools. British leaders worried that foreign workers trained in science and technical skills would beat their own.

whyNot.A: Britain kept and enlarged its empire in Asia and Africa in the late 1800s.
whyNot.B: British trade grew quickly after the repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846.
whyNot.D: Witte's push to industrialize Russia came in the 1890s, two decades after this speech.

practice.hint: Which rivals were catching up with Britain's industries around 1870?

practice.stem: The street scene in the painting is best understood as a result of which of the following?

options.A: The Paris Commune's rule over the city
options.B: Baron Haussmann's rebuilding of central Paris
options.C: Napoleon I's Continental System
options.D: The revolution of 1848 in Paris

practice.explanation: Under Napoleon III, Baron Georges Haussmann tore down crowded old neighborhoods. In their place he built wide, straight boulevards lined with matching stone apartment buildings. He also added new sewers, water pipes, parks, and gas lamps.

whyNot.A: The Paris Commune held the city for about two months in 1871 and was crushed. It did not build new streets.
whyNot.C: The Continental System (1806–1814) was Napoleon's attempt to block British trade. It was not a building plan.
whyNot.D: In 1848 Parisians built barricades in the narrow old streets. Haussmann's wide boulevards came afterward, in the 1850s and 1860s.

practice.hint: Look at the wide streets and matching buildings. Who planned Paris to look like this?

practice.stem: Wide, straight streets like the ones in the painting were built partly to

options.A: improve traffic and air and make barricades harder to build
options.B: give working-class families cheap new housing in the center of Paris
options.C: make room for large factories in the center of the city
options.D: carry new railway lines through the center of the city

practice.explanation: The new boulevards let traffic, light, and fresh air into the city. They also let troops move quickly. And they made it harder for rebels to build barricades, as Parisians had done in 1830 and 1848.

whyNot.B: The new apartment buildings had high rents. Many poorer families were pushed out toward the edges of Paris.
whyNot.C: Haussmann's projects moved factories and workshops out toward the edges of the city.
whyNot.D: Paris's railway lines ended at large stations around the edge of the old center. Trains did not run along the new boulevards.

practice.hint: Think about what had happened in Paris streets in 1830 and 1848.

practice.stem: The couple in the foreground most likely belonged to which of the following groups?

options.A: Factory workers from the suburbs
options.B: The urban bourgeoisie
options.C: Skilled artisans in workshops
options.D: Peasant migrants from the provinces

practice.explanation: The man's top hat and the woman's fur-trimmed dress and pearl earrings show that the couple is well off. They belong to the middle class, or bourgeoisie. Many such families lived in the new apartment buildings along Haussmann's boulevards.

whyNot.A: The top hat, fur trim, and pearl earrings point to a well-off family, not factory workers. Most factory workers lived in poorer areas at the edge of Paris.
whyNot.C: Some skilled artisans owned good clothes. But the couple's fine clothes, jewelry, and stroll through a new district of Paris point to the well-off bourgeoisie.
whyNot.D: Peasants who moved to Paris usually found low-paid jobs and lived in crowded housing.

practice.hint: Look at the clothing and jewelry. Who could afford them?

exam.title: Unit 6 Practice Exam: Industrialization and Its Effects
exam.directions: Each set of questions refers to a source: a primary source, a historian's writing, an image, or data. For each question, choose the best answer. Use the source and your knowledge of European history from c. 1815 to c. 1914. There is no penalty for guessing. Some sources use historical labels or words for groups of people that are no longer used; these words show the language of their time.

questions.stem: The conditions Taine describes are best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.A: The growth of state-sponsored heavy industry in Russia in the 1890s
options.B: The spread of the putting-out system, in which rural families spun and wove at home
options.C: Britain's early lead in mechanized textile production powered by coal and steam
options.D: The rise of the electrical and chemical industries of the second industrial revolution

rationales.A: Incorrect. Taine is in England, not Russia. Russia's big state-led industrial push under Sergei Witte came in the 1890s.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Taine describes huge mills with thousands of workers. Factories like these replaced the older putting-out system of home spinning and weaving.
rationales.C: Correct. Manchester was the world center of cotton manufacturing. Taine sees coal country, chimneys, and mills full of looms.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Looms, coal, and cotton mills belong to the first industrial revolution. The electrical and chemical industries grew mainly after 1870. Germany led in them.

questions.explanation: Manchester grew up around cotton mills run by steam engines that burned nearby coal. Britain led the world in this kind of factory work and became the first industrial nation. Taine describes the crowded, smoky city that resulted.

questions.stem: Taine's descriptions of the mill workers and the factory owners most directly illustrate which of the following?

options.A: The decline of the factory owners' power as landowners took over industry
options.B: The growth of an industrial working class and a wealthy owning class
options.C: The replacement of privately owned mills by state-run factories in Britain
options.D: The end of child labor in Britain's textile mills by the 1860s

rationales.A: Incorrect. Taine calls the owners "the generals and governors of human industry." Factory owners grew richer and more powerful in this period, not weaker.
rationales.B: Correct. Taine contrasts workers who go home to "hovels" with business owners whose lives are like those of "a minor prince."
rationales.C: Incorrect. Britain's mills were privately owned, as the "heads of these manufacturing or commercial houses" show.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Taine sees "men, women, and children" leaving the mills. Laws limited children's hours, but child labor did not end.

questions.explanation: Industry made the working class much larger. It also made factory owners and merchants richer and more powerful. Taine contrasts the workers' "pinched and gloomy" faces with the owners' princely power. Other groups, such as landowners, shopkeepers, and doctors and lawyers, still mattered too.

questions.stem: Conditions like those Taine describes in the workers' districts contributed most directly to which of the following later in the 1800s?

options.A: The repeal of the Corn Laws to lower the price of bread
options.B: The closing of the workhouses set up under the New Poor Law
