options.C: Public health laws and projects that built sewers and supplied clean water
options.D: Britain's adoption of protective tariffs to shield its mills from foreign rivals

rationales.A: Incorrect. The Corn Laws were repealed in 1846, before Taine's visits, as a result of the free-trade campaign.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The workhouses stayed open into the 1900s. Their system was not abolished until 1930.
rationales.C: Correct. Crowded, dirty housing spread disease. Later in the century Britain passed public health and housing laws, and cities built sewers and water systems.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Britain kept free trade until the 1930s. It did not protect its mills with tariffs.

questions.explanation: Disease and crowding in factory towns pushed Parliament and city governments to act. Laws such as the Public Health Act of 1875 made towns provide drains and clean water. Other laws let cities tear down slums.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a difference between the two sources?

options.A: Cobden says the laws favor the rich over the poor, while Disraeli warns that repeal would cost farm jobs.
options.B: Cobden says the Corn Laws protect factory jobs, while Disraeli says they make bread too costly for workers.
options.C: Cobden wants higher taxes on foreign grain, while Disraeli wants Britain to buy grain from its colonies instead.
options.D: Cobden speaks for the great landowners, while Disraeli speaks for the cotton manufacturers of Lancashire.

rationales.A: Correct. Cobden calls the duty on grain a "bread-tax" levied "for the benefit of the richest portion of the community." Disraeli worries about "displacing the labour of England that produces corn."
rationales.B: Incorrect. This reverses the sources. Cobden attacks the Corn Laws as a tax on the poor, and Disraeli defends them.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Cobden wants the "total repeal" of the taxes on food. Disraeli does not mention colonies.
rationales.D: Incorrect. This reverses the sources. Cobden was a cotton manufacturer. Disraeli defended farming against the factories of "a particular county."

questions.explanation: Cobden, a manufacturer, argued that the Corn Laws kept bread costly to protect landlords' rents. Disraeli spoke for the landowners. He argued that cheap foreign grain would ruin British farming and put farm workers out of work.

questions.stem: The debate in the two sources is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.A: Manufacturers' growing power in Parliament after the 1832 Reform Act
options.B: Napoleon's efforts to keep British goods out of continental Europe
options.C: The Chartist campaign for universal male suffrage in Britain
options.D: Reformers' campaigns to keep women and young children out of the coal mines

rationales.A: Correct. The Reform Act of 1832 gave seats to industrial towns. Manufacturers such as Cobden used their new voice to challenge the landowners who had long controlled Parliament.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Napoleon's Continental System ended when he was defeated in 1814–1815. That was decades before this debate.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The Chartists wanted the vote for all men. But neither speaker talks about who should vote. They argue about taxes on grain brought in from abroad.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Reformers won the Mines Act of 1842 to protect women and children. These sources debate the Corn Laws, not working conditions.

questions.explanation: By the 1840s, men of trade and industry had a voice in Parliament. They clashed with the landowning aristocracy. The repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846 showed how much power manufacturers had gained.

questions.stem: Cobden's argument in Source 1 most directly reflects which of the following ideologies?

options.A: Conservatism
options.B: Utopian socialism
options.C: Liberalism
options.D: Anarchism

rationales.A: Incorrect. Conservatives defended tradition and the landed interest. That was Disraeli's side of the debate.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Utopian socialists such as Robert Owen wanted communities where people shared property. Cobden defended private business.
rationales.C: Correct. Liberals such as Cobden believed in free trade and free markets and attacked special privileges, such as taxes that raised landlords' incomes.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Anarchists rejected all government. Cobden worked through Parliament to change the law.

questions.explanation: Cobden led the Anti-Corn Law League, a liberal campaign for free trade. Liberals argued that ending tariffs would lower prices and help manufacturers and workers. It would also weaken the special privileges of rich landowners.

questions.stem: By the late 1800s, which of the following developments contrasted most with the policy that Cobden urged?

options.A: Germany and France raised tariffs on grain and industrial goods.
options.B: Britain restored high Corn Law duties to protect its farmers.
options.C: Britain and France signed a treaty that lowered the tariffs between them.
options.D: Russia freed its serfs so that they could move to factory towns.

rationales.A: Correct. When railways and steamships brought cheap grain from the Americas and Russia, Germany (1879) and France (1892) raised protective tariffs. Cobden had urged free trade.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Britain did not restore the Corn Laws. It kept free trade in grain even when cheap American and Russian grain hurt British farmers in the late 1800s.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The Cobden-Chevalier Treaty of 1860 lowered tariffs. Cobden himself negotiated it, so it fit his policy.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Freeing the serfs in 1861 was about land and labor, not trade. Most freed serfs stayed bound to their village communes for years.

questions.explanation: Railways and steamships made it cheap to ship grain across oceans. During the long slump after 1873, Germany and France protected their farmers and industries with tariffs. Britain stayed with free trade.

questions.stem: The painting is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.A: Skilled craftworkers' efforts to keep production in small, hand-run workshops
options.B: The Continental System's encouragement of factories in Napoleon's empire
options.C: Prussian landowners' efforts to sell more of their estates' grain in western Europe
options.D: Prussia's rapid industrial growth, which helped it lead the unification of Germany

rationales.A: Incorrect. The painting shows a huge mill full of heavy machines and many workers. Factories like this were taking the place of small craft workshops.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The Continental System lasted from 1806 to 1814. Menzel painted this mill in the 1870s.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Landowners in eastern Prussia had long sold grain abroad. But the painting shows an ironworks, not farming.
rationales.D: Correct. Prussia's coal, iron, and railways made it the strongest German state. Menzel painted a huge ironworks in Prussian Silesia just after Germany was united under Prussia in 1871.

questions.explanation: Industry in Prussia grew fast after 1850. The Zollverein, state money for railways, and rich coal fields in the Ruhr and Silesia all helped. This strength helped Prussia unite Germany, and industry in the new German Empire kept growing fast.

questions.stem: Workers like those shown in the painting were most likely to join which of the following in the late 1800s?

options.A: Burschenschaften
options.B: Trade unions
options.C: The Anti-Corn Law League
options.D: Peasant village communes

rationales.A: Incorrect. The Burschenschaften were student clubs at universities. They were formed after 1815 to work for German unity.
rationales.B: Correct. German industrial workers joined trade unions in large numbers to bargain for higher wages, shorter hours, and safer work. Many also voted for the Social Democratic Party.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The Anti-Corn Law League was a British free-trade campaign that ended in 1846.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Village communes, such as the Russian mir, organized peasant farming, not factory work.

questions.explanation: As factories grew, workers formed trade unions and mutual aid societies. They also joined workers' parties. In Germany, unions linked to the Social Democrats had more than two million members by 1912.

questions.stem: Which conclusion about the period 1840–1860 is best supported by the data?

options.A: Railways spread earlier in the northwest, while the south and east lagged behind.
options.B: Russia's huge size let it build more miles of railway than any other country.
options.C: France added more miles of railway than the United Kingdom because its government built and ran the lines.
options.D: Spain and Italy began building railways as early as the United Kingdom did.

rationales.A: Correct. In 1840 the United Kingdom had 838 miles and tiny Belgium had 210, while Italy had 13, Russia 16, and Spain none listed. By 1860 the United Kingdom had 10,430 miles, Germany 6,980, and France 5,880. Russia, Spain, and Italy each had only about 1,000.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Russia had only 990 miles in 1860, less than one-tenth of the United Kingdom's 10,430.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The United Kingdom added about 9,600 miles, compared with about 5,500 in France. Also, private companies ran France's lines, working with the state.
rationales.D: Incorrect. In 1840 Italy had only 13 miles and Spain none listed, compared with 838 in the United Kingdom.

questions.explanation: The table shows railways spreading unevenly. By 1840 Britain, Belgium, France, and the German states already had hundreds of miles of track, while Italy, Russia, and Spain had almost none. In 1860 Russia, Spain, and Italy still had only about 1,000 miles each.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains Russia's figures for 1850 and 1860?

options.A: Russia's tsars banned the building of railways until the serfs were freed.
options.B: Serf agriculture dominated Russia's economy, leaving little capital for industry.
options.C: Russia had already built a thick network of canals and paved roads.
options.D: The Crimean War, fought on Russian soil, destroyed most of Russia's rail lines.

rationales.A: Incorrect. The tsars allowed railways: a line from St. Petersburg to Moscow opened in 1851, ten years before the serfs were freed.
rationales.B: Correct. Serfdom tied most Russians to the land, landed nobles dominated, and there was little private capital or demand for transport. These factors held back industry in eastern Europe.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Russia's roads were poor and its distances huge. That lack of transport was one reason it fell behind.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The Crimean War was fought mainly in Crimea, far from Russia's few railways. The lack of railways helped cause Russia's defeat.

questions.explanation: Serfdom, powerful landowners, huge distances, and little state support slowed industry in eastern Europe. After losing the Crimean War, Russia freed its serfs in 1861. Then it began building railways much faster.

questions.stem: The change in the figures for Germany between 1850 and 1880 is best explained by which of the following?

options.A: The end of the Zollverein, which freed each German state to build its own railways
options.B: Germany's need for railways in its colonies in Africa and the Pacific
options.C: French control of the Ruhr coal fields, which forced Germans to import coal by rail
options.D: Investment by German states in railways linking coal fields, ports, and cities

rationales.A: Incorrect. The Zollverein did not end in this period. It kept growing until the German Empire took over customs in 1871, and its free trade among the states encouraged railway building.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Germany's first colonies came in 1884, after most of this growth. The table counts railways in Europe.
rationales.C: Incorrect. France occupied the Ruhr only in 1923, long after this period.
rationales.D: Correct. German states built and backed railways, and Prussia took over most private lines after 1879. By 1880 Germany had more miles of railway than the United Kingdom.

questions.explanation: Railways tied the German states into one market. They carried coal from the Ruhr and Silesia to iron works, and they served Prussia's army. With state support, Germany passed the United Kingdom in miles of track by 1880.

questions.stem: The resolutions are best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.A: Prussia's drive to unite the German states under the Prussian king and army
options.B: The spread of socialist ideas among German factory workers and miners
options.C: Metternich's efforts to suppress liberal and nationalist ideas after 1815
options.D: Napoleon's efforts to control the press in the German lands he had conquered

rationales.A: Incorrect. Prussia joined Austria in passing the resolutions. Its push to unite Germany under its king came in the 1860s.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Socialist ideas spread among German workers later in the 1800s. The resolutions of 1819 target universities and the press.
rationales.C: Correct. Metternich called the meeting at Carlsbad after a student killed a conservative writer in 1819. The resolutions went after professors, student clubs, and the press. Those were the places where liberal and nationalist ideas spread.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Napoleon was defeated in 1815. These resolutions were passed by the German Confederation that replaced his system.

questions.explanation: After the Congress of Vienna, conservative rulers were afraid of students and professors who wanted a united Germany with a constitution. The rulers feared these Germans would start a revolution. The Carlsbad Decrees put universities under watch, censored the press, and banned student clubs.

questions.stem: Members of which of the following groups would have most strongly opposed the resolutions?

options.A: Supporters of the Holy Alliance
options.B: Prussian Junker landowners
options.C: Austrian Catholic bishops
options.D: Liberal nationalist students

rationales.A: Incorrect. The Holy Alliance of Austria, Prussia, and Russia stood for monarchy and order. Its supporters favored measures like these.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The Junkers were conservative nobles. They supported the Prussian king and feared revolution.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Austria's Catholic bishops supported the Habsburg rulers and the old order.
rationales.D: Correct. Student clubs such as the Burschenschaft wanted a united Germany with a constitution and freedom of the press. The resolutions banned their union and watched their teachers.

questions.explanation: The resolutions went after universities, student clubs, and newspapers. After 1815 these were the places where Germans who wanted a free, united Germany met and spread their ideas.

questions.stem: Which of the following later developments most directly reversed the policies in the resolutions?

options.A: The Troppau Protocol of 1820, which pledged to put down revolutions
options.B: The revolutions of 1848 and the election of the Frankfurt Parliament
options.C: The July Revolution of 1830, which ended press censorship across the German states
options.D: The founding of the Zollverein, which replaced the German Confederation

rationales.A: Incorrect. At Troppau in 1820, Austria, Prussia, and Russia agreed to act together against revolutions. That supported the policies in the resolutions instead of reversing them.
rationales.B: Correct. In March 1848 revolts forced German rulers to grant freedom of the press. The Confederation repealed the Carlsbad Decrees, and Germans elected the Frankfurt Parliament.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The July Revolution led to some new constitutions in German states. But the Confederation answered with even more controls on the press and on meetings.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The Zollverein of 1834 was a customs union. It lowered tariffs but did not replace the German Confederation.

questions.explanation: Censorship lasted in the German states until 1848. The revolutions of that year swept away the Carlsbad system for a time. But conservatives took back control in 1849.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes Engels's main argument?

options.A: Socialism became a science once it was based on economics rather than on ideals of justice.
options.B: Socialism will spread because it expresses eternal truth, reason, and justice, which conquer by their own power.
options.C: Political revolutions are caused mainly by new philosophical ideas about human rights.
options.D: Capitalism is likely to last because it rests on the natural laws of economics.

rationales.A: Correct. Engels says Marx's discoveries made socialism "a science." He says the causes of change lie "not in the philosophy, but in the economics of each particular epoch."
rationales.B: Incorrect. That is the view of the Utopians, which Engels criticizes.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Engels says the causes of revolutions are "not in men's brains" but in "changes in the modes of production and exchange."
rationales.D: Incorrect. Engels says "all social changes and political revolutions" come from "changes in the modes of production and exchange." So no economic system lasts forever. Marxists expected capitalism to be replaced.

questions.explanation: Engels says the earlier "Utopians" hoped good ideas would win people over. Marx, he says, made socialism "a science" by explaining history through the way goods are made and traded and through the struggle between classes.

questions.stem: Which of the following thinkers would Engels most likely have classified among the "Utopians"?

options.A: Charles Fourier
options.B: Mikhail Bakunin
options.C: John Stuart Mill
options.D: Friedrich List

rationales.A: Correct. Fourier planned model communities based on reason and justice. In this pamphlet Engels discusses him, Henri de Saint-Simon, and Robert Owen as the leading Utopians.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Bakunin was an anarchist who opposed all government. Marx and Engels fought with him in the First International around 1870, but over the state, not over plans for ideal communities.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Mill was a liberal thinker. He was not a socialist who planned ideal communities.
rationales.D: Incorrect. List was an economist. He wanted tariffs to protect and build German industry.

questions.explanation: Engels named Saint-Simon, Fourier, and Owen as the leading utopian socialists. In the early 1800s they attacked the new industrial society and planned a better one. Fourier and Owen designed model communities. Engels said their plans rested on reason and justice, not on a scientific study of history and class.

questions.stem: Engels's ideas are best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.A: The restoration of absolute monarchies by the Congress of Vienna
options.B: The Romantic movement's emphasis on emotion and the beauty of nature
options.C: The growth of an industrial working class and of socialist movements
options.D: The breakdown of the Concert of Europe during the Crimean War of 1853–1856

rationales.A: Incorrect. The Congress of Vienna met in 1814–1815. Engels writes about the economic causes of social change in the late 1800s.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Romanticism stressed feeling and nature. Engels stresses economics and science.
rationales.C: Correct. By 1880 factories had created a large working class, and socialist parties and unions were growing. Engels wanted to give their movement a scientific theory.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The Crimean War (1853–1856) concerned the great powers and the Ottoman Empire, not class and production.

questions.explanation: Capitalist industry created a large working class, or proletariat, and sharp divisions between classes. Socialists such as Marx and Engels said they could explain these changes scientifically. They predicted that workers would replace capitalism.

questions.stem: Members of which of the following groups would most likely have agreed with Engels's criticism of the Utopians?

options.A: The Anti-Corn Law League
options.B: Owen's cooperative societies
options.C: The German Social Democratic Party
options.D: The Chartist movement

rationales.A: Incorrect. The Anti-Corn Law League was a liberal free-trade campaign of the 1840s, not a socialist group.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Owen was one of the Utopians Engels criticized, so his followers would have defended his ideas.
rationales.C: Correct. In 1891 the German Social Democrats adopted the Erfurt Program, which was based on Marx's ideas. It became Europe's largest workers' party.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The Chartists of 1838–1848 sought political rights for workers through the People's Charter. Their movement grew before Marx's ideas were widely known.

questions.explanation: Marx's ideas shaped the large socialist parties of the late 1800s. Engels advised the German Social Democratic Party. It built its program on the "scientific" socialism he describes.

questions.stem: Chadwick's argument that public works "would be a pecuniary gain" was most likely intended to

options.A: convince doctors that disease was spread by germs carried in water
options.B: argue that the generous poor relief of the old Poor Law should be restored
options.C: persuade Parliament to raise wages for workers in unhealthy trades
options.D: persuade lawmakers worried about cost that sanitation would save money

rationales.A: Incorrect. Chadwick blames "atmospheric impurities" from filth. The germ theory of disease was developed later, by Louis Pasteur and others.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Chadwick helped write the New Poor Law of 1834, which made relief harder to get. He did not want the old system back.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Chadwick says prosperity and good wages did not protect workers from disease. He asks for drains and water, not higher wages.
rationales.D: Correct. Many officials disliked new spending. Chadwick argues that drains and clean water would cut the cost of sickness and early death.

questions.explanation: Chadwick knew that Parliament and taxpayers worried about cost. He argued that drains, garbage removal, and clean water would pay for themselves. They would cut the costs of sickness and of caring for widows and orphans.

questions.stem: Chadwick's report most directly contributed to which of the following?

options.A: A Public Health Act creating a General Board of Health
options.B: A national insurance system that paid for workers' medical care
options.C: A New Poor Law that set up workhouses for the poor
options.D: A Reform Act that gave the vote to more middle-class men

rationales.A: Correct. The Public Health Act of 1848 followed Chadwick's report. Chadwick sat on the General Board of Health it created.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Britain set up national health insurance for workers only in 1911, long after the report. It followed Germany's example.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The New Poor Law of 1834 came before the report. Chadwick helped design it, but it dealt with poor relief.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The Reform Act of 1832 came before the report and changed voting, not public health.

questions.explanation: The report showed how filth and bad water killed thousands. It led to the Public Health Act of 1848, which let towns set up local boards of health to build drains and water supplies.

questions.stem: The conditions described in the report were most directly caused by

options.A: enclosure, which forced landowners to move into towns
options.B: the end of poor relief, which left the poor without any help
options.C: the Irish potato famine, which spread disease to British cities
options.D: the rapid growth of towns as people left the countryside for work

rationales.A: Incorrect. Enclosure pushed many poor rural laborers off the land, not landowners into towns.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Poor relief continued under the New Poor Law of 1834, though it became harsher.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The famine began in 1845, three years after this report.
rationales.D: Correct. Industrial towns grew faster than anyone built drains, water supplies, or decent housing, so many people crowded into "close and overcrowded dwellings."

questions.explanation: As factories grew, people poured into towns from the countryside. Cities could not keep up. Crowding, poor drains, and dirty water spread disease.

questions.stem: In addition to the French example described in the passage, which of the following contributed most to the outbreak of the revolutions of 1848?

options.A: The defeat of Austria and Prussia in a war against France in 1847
options.B: Bad harvests and an economic slump in 1846–1847
options.C: Marxist parties that had won seats in most European parliaments
options.D: The freeing of the Russian serfs, which inspired peasants elsewhere

rationales.A: Incorrect. There was no war between France and the German powers in 1847. France, Austria, and Prussia had not fought one another since 1815.
rationales.B: Correct. Potato blight, poor grain harvests, and a business slump left many people hungry and out of work. Hardship joined discontent with the political order.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Marx and Engels published The Communist Manifesto in February 1848. No Marxist party yet held seats in any parliament.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Russia freed its serfs in 1861, after the revolutions of 1848.

questions.explanation: Two things set off the revolutions of 1848. Bad harvests and lost jobs left many people hungry, and liberals and nationalists were angry at the old rulers.

questions.stem: Which of the following best supports Seignobos's claim that in some places the revolutions "took the form of a nationalist movement"?

options.A: Paris workers rose against the government in the June Days after the national workshops closed.
options.B: Hungarians led by Lajos Kossuth demanded self-rule and fought the Austrian army.
options.C: Chartists in London presented a final petition for universal male suffrage.
options.D: Louis Napoleon was elected president of the French Republic in December 1848.

rationales.A: Incorrect. The June Days were a fight between Paris workers and the republic's government. It was a class conflict, not a nationalist movement.
rationales.B: Correct. Hungarian nationalists wanted their own government within, and later outside, the Habsburg empire. They fought until Russian troops helped Austria defeat them in 1849.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The Chartists wanted the vote for all men in Britain. They were not fighting for national independence or national unity.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Louis Napoleon was elected in France. His election was not a nationalist uprising.

questions.explanation: In 1848 Hungarians, Italians, Czechs, and Germans wanted to rule themselves or to unite their nations. Kossuth led the Hungarian revolt against the Habsburgs, who ruled Austria.

questions.stem: The events described in the last two paragraphs most directly show that by 1849

options.A: the revolutions had united Germany under a liberal constitution
options.B: Russia had joined the liberal powers in supporting national independence
options.C: Metternich had restored the Concert of Europe to its full strength
options.D: conservative monarchs could still crush revolutions with their armies and allies

rationales.A: Incorrect. The Frankfurt Parliament "dispersed." Germany was not united until 1871.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The Russian tsar sent his army to crush the Hungarian revolution.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Metternich was driven from power in March 1848 and fled Austria. The Concert of Europe never recovered its old strength.
rationales.D: Correct. Prussian armies crushed the German democrats, and a Russian army conquered Hungary for Austria. The old rulers regained control.

questions.explanation: By 1849 the revolutions had failed almost everywhere. Conservative rulers used their armies, sometimes with foreign help, to restore order. The Concert of Europe had broken down, and Metternich was gone.
